summary:
The change touches one file, `src/View/Shortcodes/EmbedShortcodeProvider.php` (Silverstripe's `[embed]` shortcode handler). It deletes the private helper `removeDangerousAttributes()` and changes the "simple single iframe" fast path in `sandboxHtml()` to `return $html;` unchanged.

I read the file in full to establish the trust model and the data flow. `sandboxHtml()` is the security boundary for third-party oEmbed markup: anything it does not recognise is re-wrapped into a `data:text/html` iframe carrying the configured `sandboxed_iframe_attributes`, so remote HTML cannot execute in the site's origin. Only two paths escape that wrapping — the configured domain exclusion at line 382, and the single-iframe fast path at lines 386-393. I traced the source (`$extractor->code->html`, i.e. markup returned by whatever remote server the embedded URL resolves to, reached via `handle_shortcode` → `embeddableToHtml` → `videoEmbed`) and the sink (`DBField::create_field('HTMLFragment', $content)` at line 228, rendered unescaped by design).

Findings, both reported:

1. The fast path now emits provider-controlled iframe markup verbatim. The remaining guards (`^<iframe[^>]*>`, `</iframe\s*>$`, `substr_count($html, '<') <= 2`) constrain only tag shape and `<` count, not attributes, so `onload=` / `onerror=` handlers and entity-encoded `srcdoc` payloads now pass through to the page's own origin. The deleted helper was exactly the control that removed them, via an attribute allowlist plus rejection of `javascript:`/`data:`/`vbscript:`/`file:` schemes on `src`. Reported as introduced by this change.

2. Pre-existing, in the exclusion gate I had to read to settle reachability: `domainIsExcludedFromSandboxing()` uses `str_ends_with()` with no label boundary, so a configured `youtube.com` also matches an attacker-registered `evilyoutube.com`, bypassing sandboxing entirely. Rated medium/low-confidence because the declared default for the setting is an empty array and no site configuration is present in this repository.

One related symptom I did not report separately: the width/height `preg_replace` in `videoEmbed()` (lines 206-214) interpolates the shortcode's `width`/`height` arguments into the markup without escaping, so a value like `1" onload="...` can inject an attribute. Before this change that was neutralised by `removeDangerousAttributes()` on the fast path and by the data-URI wrapping otherwise; it becomes live only through the same root cause as finding 1, so I folded it into that finding rather than duplicating it.

I did not manufacture additional issues — the rest of the file (cache key derivation, attribute allowlisting in `buildAttributeListFromArguments`, the `linkEmbed`/`photoEmbed` paths) is unchanged and uses `Convert::raw2att` appropriately.
unresolved: The repository as provided contains only src/View/Shortcodes/EmbedShortcodeProvider.php — no templates, no YAML config, no routing or permission layer. I could not read the EmbedShortcodeProvider_video template to confirm with my own eyes that Content is emitted unescaped, nor confirm the HTMLFragment casting behaviour from source; both are inferred from Silverstripe's documented semantics for HTMLFragment.

Because no routing or CMS permission code is visible, I could not determine who is allowed to author an [embed] shortcode on a given install, so reachable_without_authentication is recorded as 'unclear' on both findings. On a stock CMS this requires an authenticated content author; on a site that renders user-submitted HTMLText it could be unauthenticated.

I could not see any real site configuration for domains_excluded_from_sandboxing. Finding 2 is unexploitable at the declared default (empty array) and depends entirely on deployment configuration I could not inspect.

I could not check the project's test suite for cases asserting that dangerous attributes are stripped from the fast path — no tests exist in this corpus — so I could not confirm whether this deletion was a deliberate revert accompanied by a compensating control elsewhere in the wider codebase.

findings.title: Removal of iframe attribute sanitiser allows stored XSS via embed shortcode
findings.severity_derivation: state_change → high; needs a victim to act → medium
findings.description:
`sandboxHtml()` is the security boundary for third-party oEmbed markup: everything it does not recognise is wrapped into a `data:text/html` iframe with the configured `sandboxed_iframe_attributes`, so remote HTML never executes in the site's origin. The one exception is the "simple single iframe" fast path at lines 386-393, which returns the provider's markup to be rendered directly into the page.

Before this change that fast path was still filtered by `removeDangerousAttributes()`, which stripped every attribute outside a strict allowlist (`src`, `width`, `height`, `frameborder`, `allow`, `allowfullscreen`, `referrerpolicy`, `loading`, `scrolling`, `allowtransparency`, `title`) and additionally rejected `src` values whose scheme was `javascript`, `data`, `vbscript` or `file`. The diff deletes that method and replaces the call with `return $html;`, so the raw remote markup is now emitted unmodified.

The guard conditions do not substitute for attribute filtering. `preg_match('#^<iframe[^>]*>#')`, `preg_match('#</iframe\s*>$#')` and `substr_count($html, '<') <= 2` only constrain the tag shape and the number of `<` characters; they place no constraint whatsoever on which attributes appear on the iframe. Markup such as `<iframe src="https://example.com/" onload="..."></iframe>` contains exactly two `<` characters and satisfies both regexes, so it now flows straight through.

The sink is in `videoEmbed()` at line 224-228: the returned string is passed to `sandboxHtml()` and then cast with `DBField::create_field('HTMLFragment', $content)`, which Silverstripe renders unescaped by design, placing the attacker's iframe in the page's own origin. Two payload families are immediately available: an inline event handler (`onload`/`onerror`), which executes in the parent document's context, and `srcdoc` with entity-encoded markup (`<iframe srcdoc="<script>...</script>"></iframe>`, still only two `<` characters), which renders a same-origin document. Both were previously removed by the attribute allowlist.

Note that `domainIsExcludedFromSandboxing()` is a separate, explicitly configured opt-out; it is not what makes this path safe, and it returns early at line 382 before this code is reached.
findings.exploit_scenario: A content author (a role normally below administrator) inserts `[embed url="https://attacker.example/page"]` into a page body. Resolving the shortcode causes the server to fetch that URL and take the oEmbed provider's `code->html` as the embed markup, so the attacker controls that string exactly. The attacker's server returns `<iframe src="https://attacker.example/v" onload="fetch('/admin/security/add',{...})"></iframe>`. This starts with `<iframe...>`, ends with `</iframe>`, and contains two `<` characters, so it takes the fast path at line 390-391 and is returned verbatim instead of being attribute-filtered. It is then rendered as an `HTMLFragment` into the published page. When an administrator views that page in the CMS preview or on the front end, the `onload` handler runs in the site's origin with the admin's session, letting the attacker perform authenticated actions as that administrator. The same holds without any malicious author if a legitimate third-party oEmbed provider is compromised — that untrusted-provider case is precisely why the sandbox exists.
findings.recommendation: Restore attribute filtering on the unsandboxed fast path rather than returning `$html` unchanged — reinstate `removeDangerousAttributes()` (allowlist of attribute names plus rejection of `javascript:`/`data:`/`vbscript:`/`file:` in `src`), and ensure `srcdoc` is not on the allowlist. A more robust alternative is to stop trusting the provider's markup entirely: parse the iframe, extract only the `src` URL, validate its scheme against `https`/`http`, and rebuild the tag with `HTML::createTag('iframe', [...])` from known-safe attributes, so no provider-supplied attribute is ever echoed. Regex-based shape checks such as `substr_count($html, '<') <= 2` should not be relied on as a sanitisation control.

findings.title: Sandbox exclusion uses unanchored domain suffix match (pre-existing)
findings.severity_derivation: state_change → high; needs a victim to act → medium
findings.description:
This is pre-existing code the diff does not modify, but it is the first gate in `sandboxHtml()` and I had to read it to establish whether the changed fast path was reachable, so I am reporting it.

`domainIsExcludedFromSandboxing()` compares the host of the resolved embed URL against each configured excluded domain with `str_ends_with($domain, $excludedDomain)`. The comparison has no label boundary: it matches on a raw string suffix rather than on a dot-delimited subdomain boundary. Configuring `youtube.com` therefore also matches hosts such as `evilyoutube.com`, `myyoutube.com` or `notyoutube.com`, all of which an attacker can register.

When this returns true, `sandboxHtml()` returns at line 382-384 with the provider's markup completely untouched — it never reaches the iframe shape checks or (previously) the attribute allowlist. So a suffix collision yields unrestricted HTML injection into the page, which is strictly broader than the fast-path issue reported separately.

The declared default for `domains_excluded_from_sandboxing` in this file is an empty array, so a default installation is unaffected; exploitation requires a site that has configured at least one exclusion, which is the intended use of the setting. I could not see any site configuration in this repository, which is why I am not rating this higher.
findings.exploit_scenario: A site configures `SilverStripe\View\Shortcodes\EmbedShortcodeProvider.domains_excluded_from_sandboxing: ['youtube.com']` so that YouTube embeds render natively. An attacker registers `evilyoutube.com` and serves an oEmbed endpoint there. A content author (or the attacker, on any site where embed URLs can be supplied by a lower-privileged user) inserts `[embed url="https://evilyoutube.com/watch?v=1"]`. `parse_url` yields host `evilyoutube.com`; `str_ends_with('evilyoutube.com', 'youtube.com')` is true, so `sandboxHtml()` returns the attacker's markup verbatim at line 383 with no shape or attribute checks at all. The attacker's oEmbed response returns arbitrary HTML — for example a `<script>` tag or an element with an inline event handler — which is rendered as an `HTMLFragment` into the page and executes in the site's origin when any visitor or administrator views it.
findings.recommendation: Match on a domain boundary rather than a bare string suffix, and accept an exact match: e.g. `if ($domain === $excludedDomain || str_ends_with($domain, '.' . $excludedDomain))`. Normalise both sides to lower case and strip any trailing dot before comparing so that `YouTube.com` and `youtube.com.` are handled consistently.
